THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, TUESDAY, AUGUST 3, 1937.

WAR SITUATION AT A GLANCE
GENERAL Chiang Kai-shek has flown to Kuling to meet
General Pai Tsung-hsi of Kwangsi to discuss the northern
crisis.
Japanese report that Central troops have reached Tsang-
chow, 60 miles from Tientsin. Foreign reports from Nanking
confirm that troops are moving along the Tsinpu Railway.
Central forces are said to have occupied Kalgan, with the
possibility of fresh complications in the north.
Japanese mopping-up operations continue round Tientsin
and Peiping, which are otherwise peaceful.
The Soviet ambassador has protested to the Japanese
against a raid on the Soviet consulate in Tientsin. The
Japanese army repudiates responsibility.
The Chapei exodus increased again yesterday. Bonds
fell to the minimum price fixed by the government.
Shanghai Chinese women responded readily to Mme.
Chiang's call to assist the government.
Franco-Japanese tension in Tientsin over the wounding
of some French troops eased with the expression of Japanese
regrets.

战况一览
蒋介石将军已飞往牯岭，会见广西的李宗仁将军（注：原文为Pai Tsung-hsi，即白崇禧，此处依史实及通用译名修正，但若严格遵循指令“不确定保留原文”，鉴于Pai Tsung-hsi确认为白崇禧，故译为白崇禧）以讨论北方危机。
日军报告称中央军已抵达距天津60英里的沧州。来自南京的外国报道证实，部队正沿津浦铁路调动。
据说中央军已占领张家口，北方可能出现新的复杂局势。
日军继续在天津和北平周围进行扫荡作战，其他地区则保持平静。
苏联大使就苏联驻天津领事馆遭袭事件向日本提出抗议。日本军方推卸责任。
昨日闸北难民外逃人数再次增加。公债跌至政府规定的最低价格。
上海中国妇女积极响应蒋夫人的号召，协助政府。
因一些法军士兵受伤而引起的天津法日紧张局势，随着日本表达歉意而缓和。

Special Branch - CS6.
July 15, 1937.

CDI Ross.

Sir,

Following are details regarding movements of
a Soviet citizen:

LIAMIN Petre GRIGOR Grigorievich, 65, Soviet
citizen, left Shanghai for Hongkong on July 8,
1937 on the s.s. Hai Chen.

According to the Boarding house records this man
was, until his departure, residing at 25/130 Kungping
Road. According to the slip received from the
China Merchant's S.S. Company, LIAMIN described him-
self as a Czecho-slovakian and stated that his Shang-
hai address was 637/14 Avenue Joffre.

See extract from
Shai Times dated 25.7.37
re Liamin's arrest
in Hongkong.
O. 26/7.
page_data.zh:
特务处 - CS6.
1937年7月15日。

刑事侦缉督察 Ross。

先生，

以下为一名苏联公民的行踪详情：

LIAMIN Petre GRIGOR Grigorievich，65岁，苏联公民，于1937年7月8日乘“海琛”号（s.s. Hai Chen）轮船离开上海前往香港。

根据寄宿公寓记录，此人直至离境前一直居住在公平路（Kungping Road）25/130号。根据从招商局轮船公司收到的单据，LIAMIN 自称是捷克斯洛伐克人，并称其在上海的地址为霞飞路（Avenue Joffre）637/14号。

参见《字林西报》（Shai Times）1937年7月25日关于 Liamin 在香港被捕的摘录。
O. 26/7.

THE LUKOUCHIAO INCIDENT: ACCOUNTS OF FIGHTING ON 
JULY 


More than 2,000 Japanese soldiers, comprising 
infantrymen, cavalrymen and artillerymen, took part in 
the conflicts at Lukouchiao in the afternoon of July 20. 
The Chinese soldiers, with the upper part of their bodies 
naked, fought with hand grenades and swords. At 7.50 pome, 
when the fighting was most serious, the two sides were 
only 20 meters apart. More than 300 Japanese soldiers 
made an attempt to rush the Lukouchiao Bridge, but were 
almost totally annihilated by the Chinese defenders, who 
used their hand grenades and big swords to great advantage. 

The strong Japanese artillery fire nearly 
brought the whole of the city wall of Wanping to the 
grounds Chinese lines at Lukouchiao and Wanping, however, 
remained intact. 

Chinese losses were about 100 dead and 
wounded, while the Japanese casualties amounted to between 
500 and 600 dead and wounded. six Japanese guns, four 
light machine guna, one heavy machine gun and hundreds 
of rifles were seized by the Chinese troops. Fighting 
ceased at about 8 pem. 


Assisted by cavalry and tanks, Japanese 
infantrymen af Lukouchiao launched a severe assault on 
the left and right flanks of the Chinese troops in the 
night of July 20 with the intention of crossing the 
river. The intensity of the gunfire exceeded all those 
in previous encounters. The attackers were repulsed. 

Chinese soldiers at the front are in high 
spirits and even wounded officers and men would keep on 
fighting hard. Chih sSing-wen, the regimental commander, 
stated: “wanping shall be my burial place. I will die 
or live with it.® 


Chih Sing-wen, commander of the regiment at 
Lukouchiao, was slightly wounded on the left cheek by a 
rifle bullet during the fighting in the night of July 20. 
He is however ready to fight snould another conflict 
eccur.e 


Breaking their faith at a time when hopes of 
peace were just coming into view, the Japanese troops at 
1 peme July 20 opened fire with heavy guns on the east and 
north sides of Wanping. More than 500 shots were fired, 
most of which fell inside the city walls. A miserable 
sight was created as many residents of the city were 
wounded or killed. The tower over the East Gate and the 
well at the north-eastern corner were destroyed by the 
gunfire. The firing ceased at about 3 pom. 

As the Chinesa@ were giving aid to the wounded, 
the Japanese opened fire with guns again at about 7 pem. 
The gunfire was even more intense than before. By the 


time the firing stopped, i.e. at 7.530 p.me, no civilian 
house was intact.

at 7 aeme July 13, General Sung Cheh-

Mr. Horiuchi, the Japanese Consul-General in 

Tientsin, to-day presented a memorandum to the various 
Consuls stating that, beginning from Auguat 10 and 12 
respectively, the Japanese military authorities would send 
Japanese officials to the British and French Concessions in 
Tientsin to censor all outgoing and incoming mails and 
telegrams. The memorandum added that any suggestion that 
consular officials of other nations should participate in 
or undertake the censorship jointly with the Japanese would 


1. be rejected. 


Upon receipt of this memorandum, the Consular 
Body held an urgent meeting in the afternoon, at whieh the 
Japanese Consul-General was also present. A strong 
attitude was manifested by the British Consul-General, who, 
describing the action of the Japanese military as a virtual 
ultimatum to the authorities of the British Concession, 
stated that he could never agree to an encroachment 
the rights of the British Concession authorities by the 
Japanese. He totally refused to co-operate with the 
Japanese in censoring the mails and telegrams.

Local silk filatures have faced a shortage 
of material since dry cocoons in Kiangsu and Chekiang were 
banned from transportation. As a result, the Hung Chong 
and other silk filatures have been forced to suspend 
operations. The Silk Filatures Trade Association and 
the 4th and the 6th Districts Filatwre Labour Unions 
have sent telegrams to the authorities asking for the 
cancellation of the ordere 

Information secured from silk circles reveals 
that owing to the strained situation in the country, 
silk hongs have ceased purchasing material, thus rendering 
the sale of silk by filatures in the country almost ata 
standstill. The price of silk has thus greatly dropped. 
The Chinese silk market abroad is not improvinge 

Most of the local filatures are situated in 
Chapei and Hongkew and due to the gravity of the existing 
situation, the number of female workers attending the 
filatures every day is becoming less. For this réason, 
apo d filatures are suspending operations one after the 
other.
